title: The Scammer's Playbook
intro: Meet the four feelings scammers press again and again: urgency, fear, greed and false trust. You will practise naming them in real-looking messages.
recap: Most scams work on a feeling, not a machine. Scammers press urgency, fear, greed and trust.
A genuine problem can almost always wait ten minutes while you check it properly.
A message that knows your name is not proof that it is real.
You never pay a fee to receive a prize or money you did not ask for.

aiTutor.recap: Most scammers do not break into your phone or your bank. They get you to hand over the key yourself, by making you feel something strongly enough to act before you think. This lesson names the four feelings they rely on, so you can spot them in any message.
aiTutor.example: Ada's text said her account would be blocked in 30 minutes. She did not stop to ask who sent it. She typed her details into a page that looked real, and the scammer never touched her phone.
aiTutor.watchOut: It is easy to think only careless people fall for this. Scammers design their messages to work on careful people too, so being rushed is not a sign that you are foolish.
aiTutor.tryThis: Think of the last message that made your heart jump. Which feeling was it using?

glossary.definition: A trick that gets you to give away money or private details willingly, because you believe a lie. The word covers calls, texts, emails, social media messages and face-to-face tricks.
glossary.example: A text saying you won a prize, but you must send a fee first, is a scam.

glossary.definition: Broken into by technical means, for example when software gets past a password. Most scams skip this step and simply ask you for what they need.
glossary.example: Hacking: someone guesses a weak password. A scam: someone phones and asks you to read out your code.

paragraphs: Here is a made-up story. Ada gets a text: "Your bank account will be blocked in 30 minutes. Tap here to fix it." Her heart jumps. She taps, types her details, and a minute later her money is gone.
Nobody hacked Ada's phone. Ada was rushed and scared, and she gave the scammer exactly what he wanted. That is how most scams work. The weak point is a feeling, not a machine.
Good news: scammers use the same few feelings again and again. Once you can name them, you can spot them, and pause before you act. That is what this course is for.

aiTutor.explain: Tap each lever and notice how it feels. Real scam messages rarely use only one. A threat with a deadline pulls fear and urgency together, which is why such messages work so well.
aiTutor.example: "Your account will be closed today unless you confirm your PIN." This one line uses fear (a closed account), urgency (today) and trust (it pretends to be your bank).
aiTutor.watchOut: A message does not need to look suspicious to be a scam. Good scams are polite, well spelled and look official.
aiTutor.tryThis: Take a message you received this week and tick which of the four levers it uses.

walkThrough.title: Taking apart one message: "Your account will be closed today unless you confirm your PIN."
steps: Fear: the message threatens a closed account, which makes your heart jump.
Urgency: the word "today" gives you a deadline, so you feel you cannot wait.
Trust: it sounds like your bank, so your guard goes down.
Three levers in one line. That is a sign to slow down, not a reason to hurry.
What to do instead: do not reply or tap anything. Open your bank's own app, or call the number on your card, and ask whether there is a problem.

nodes.label: Urgency
nodes.title: Urgency: "Act now!"
nodes.definition: A deadline stops you from thinking. "Within 30 minutes", "last chance", "today only". Real problems rarely need an answer in minutes.
nodes.bonusFact: Rushing you is the scammer's main tool, because a calm person asks questions. Whenever a deadline appears, treat it as a reason to slow down, not to speed up.

nodes.label: Fear
nodes.title: Fear: "Something bad will happen"
nodes.definition: Threats of a blocked account, a lost job, arrest or a family emergency make you act before you check.
nodes.bonusFact: Frightened people tend to follow instructions, which is exactly what the scammer needs. If a message scares you, contact the real organisation yourself, using details you already trust.

nodes.label: Greed
nodes.title: Greed: "Easy money!"
nodes.definition: A prize, a free gift or big returns with no risk. You want it to be true, so you stop looking for the catch.
nodes.bonusFact: Wanting something good is normal, and scammers aim at that wish. A useful question to ask: why would a stranger give me this for free?

nodes.label: Trust
nodes.title: Trust: "I am someone you know"
nodes.definition: The sender pretends to be your bank, a relative, an employer or a friend, so your guard goes down.
nodes.bonusFact: A name, a logo or a familiar voice can all be copied, so they prove nothing on their own. Confirm through a second route, such as calling the person on a number you already have.

widgetData.completionMessage: You have met all four levers: urgency, fear, greed and trust.
widgetData.completionBonusFact: Most scam messages pull at least two of these levers at the same time. Counting the levers in a message is a quick way to judge how risky it is.

aiTutor.explain: Read the message again and ask two questions: what does it want me to feel, and what does it want me to do? Here it dangles a prize, which is the feeling, and asks for money today, which is the action.
aiTutor.watchOut: Do not be distracted by how large the prize is. The size of the offer is part of the bait.

widgetData.question: A message says: "You won 500,000 naira in our mobile draw! Send 5,000 naira today to unlock your prize." Which lever is it pulling most?

options.text: Fear: it threatens you with something bad.
Greed: it offers a prize you did not earn, and a deadline.
Trust: it comes from someone you know.

widgetData.explanation: A prize for a draw you never entered is the bait, and "today" adds a deadline. A real prize never asks you to pay first. If you had truly won, the organiser would not need your money to hand over theirs.
widgetData.bonusFact: Asking you to pay a fee to receive money is one of the oldest scam patterns. If you are tempted, search for the exact wording of the message online. Others have often posted about the same trick.

aiTutor.explain: Decide whether each statement is true or false. Think about how a real company or a real friend behaves: they are patient, they let you check, and they never ask you to pay to receive something.
aiTutor.tryThis: For each card, picture a real bank clerk or a real friend. Would they say or do this?

widgetData.instruction: Is each statement true or false?

cards.statement: A genuine problem with your account can almost always wait ten minutes while you check it properly.
cards.explanation: Real organisations give you time and several ways to confirm. Checking first costs you nothing.
cards.bonusFact: Try saying "I will call you back on the number on my card." A real caller will accept that.

cards.statement: If a message uses your correct name, it must be real.
cards.explanation: Names are easy to find or buy. A message that knows your name can still be a scam.
cards.bonusFact: A scammer knowing your name is like a stranger knowing your street. It proves nothing about who they are.

cards.statement: A message that makes you feel scared or excited is a reason to slow down.
cards.explanation: Strong feelings are the lever. Pausing takes the power out of it.
cards.bonusFact: Count to ten and ask one other person before you reply or pay.

cards.statement: A real prize can ask you to pay a small fee before you receive it.
cards.explanation: Paying first to get money is the trap. The "fee" is what the scammer is after.
cards.bonusFact: A good rule: you never pay money to receive money you did not ask for.

screens.title: Match the Message to the Lever

aiTutor.review: Match each made-up message to the lever it pulls most. Look at the feeling the message wants from you, not only at its words.
aiTutor.watchOut: Some messages mix levers. Choose the one that pushes hardest. A deadline wants you to hurry, a threat wants you scared, a sure win wants you hopeful, and a familiar voice wants you relaxed.

widgetData.instruction: Match each message to the lever it uses most:

pairs.left: "Reply in 10 minutes or lose this offer"
"Your account will be closed and reported"
"Hi, it is me, I changed my number"

widgetData.explanation: A deadline is urgency, a threat is fear, a big sure win is greed, and a familiar voice or number is trust.
widgetData.bonusFact: When a message arrives, name the feeling it gives you before you answer. Naming it makes it easier to pause.

aiTutor.review: One habit beats all four levers. Fill in the blank with it. It works because every lever depends on you acting fast.
aiTutor.tryThis: Next time a message rushes you, put your phone down for ten minutes and then decide.

widgetData.template: When a message rushes or scares you, the safest first move is to {blank} before you act.
widgetData.explanation: Pausing breaks the lever. It gives you time to check using a number or app you already trust, and a scammer's plan depends on you having no time.
widgetData.bonusFact: Telling a friend or family member about a strange message is a quick way to see it clearly. A second pair of eyes is not rushed by the same feeling.
